newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FOCUS-New Romania rules baffle foreign investors.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New Romania rules baffle foreign investors.

text.p: Romania's government baffled foreign investors on Monday by announcing revisions to proposed portfolio investment rules, introducing what some analysts said was a prohibitve tax on transactions.

"This makes the Romanian market significantly more expensive than others," Mark Holdsworth of ING Barings in London told Reuters by telephone. "If it goes through, it would be a big block on the development of volumes on the exchange."

Reform Minister Ulm Spineanu said on Monday the cabinet had introduced a 1.5 percent tax on each portfolio transaction to replace a four percent tax for repatriating capital gains and an additional 0.1 percent tax on short-term flows.
He said the latest amendment was intended to allay fears that a capital gains fee might act as a barrier when investors considered leaving the market.
"We decided to have a single tax as a simple rule seems more favourable for foreign investors and it is easier to monitor," Spineanu told Reuters.
Analysts suggested many investors would now be wary in committing funds to the Balkan country.
"What they are actually doing is compelling you to stay in the market on the longer term so you make more money to cover the taxes," a Western analyst said.

Adoption of a law on portfolio investment had been viewed as a critical measure in pressing forward with the reforms launched by the centrist government in February and attracting the interest of previously uneasy Western investors.

Investors initially welcomed the proposed law when a government statement said it had been adopted last week. The announcement coincided with a monitoring mission to Bucharest by the International Monetary Fund and discussions by the World Bank board in Washington on releasing credits.
A government official said the latest amendments would be discussed by the government and be published in the Official Gazette before becoming effective.
"It seems the government is not coherent on this issue," the Western analyst said. "They are addressing the issue but in a way that does not guarantee the (investment) regime will remain stable."
Some economists said the new taxes made investments in Romania more expensive than in its ex-communist neighbours.

"The new tax is higher compared with other countries in Eastern Europe, like for instance the Czech Republic. This means Romania does not plan to compete with other markets in the region," a foreign economist said.
Bucharest stock exchange officials and brokers predicted the move would have a negative impact on equities.
"Since last week, when they first announced the draft, we have had stronger volumes. Now, with the market bound to turn costly, foreigners may start to retreat," a trader said.

"With the new tax, plus brokers' commissions of up to two percent and the exchange's own 0.3 percent fee, Romania will be no heaven for foreign investors," said Doru Nicolaescu, a member of the stock exchange committee.
But some investors were less worried about tax rates than creating a stable investment climate.
"I don't think these taxes are anything to worry about," a London analyst said. "What's really worrying is that the government seems unable to make a decision and implement it."

"What certainly alerts foreign investors are potential changes in the foreign investment regime, which at some stage might become retroactive," said David Boren, vice-president of Salomon Brothers in London.
